The bet for Richard: buy a business whose earnings are close to certain for eighteen months, at a multiple 15% to 18% below its normal level, and let the market's slow recognition of that certainty supply the rest of the return. Definitions, sources and the basis of every figure are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: the case, what drives it, and the five judgements that move the shares

RELX's earnings are among the most predictable in European equities, yet in 2026 the market priced the shares as if those earnings were among the least predictable. RELX has delivered about 7% underlying revenue growth for sixteen years, with a margin gain in every year, cash conversion of 97% to 100% and no guidance cut outside the 2020 closure of trade shows.

Two forces cut the multiple, and neither has touched the earnings. RELX's two-year-forward P/E fell from 27x in April 2025 to 14.3x in June 2026. The first force was a sector-wide fear that AI-native tools will disintermediate professional databases: RELX's shares fell 14.7% in one day when Anthropic launched a legal plug-in on 3 February 2026. The second force was a rise in bond yields, which Bernstein estimates explains about half of the de-rating.

The recovery is only part-way through. Since the February low of 2,013p the shares have risen 51%, and the multiple is back to about 18x. That level is roughly the ten-year median but still only the 15th percentile of the last five years.

The model compounds adjusted EPS at 10% to 12% a year (143p in FY26, 158p in FY27, 177p in FY28 and 196p in FY29). The compounding rests on 7% underlying revenue growth, an operating margin rising about 50 to 60 basis points a year to 37.8% by FY30, and buybacks of £1.75bn to £2.0bn a year at constant leverage. At the guideline fair multiple of 20.84x, the model's total shareholder return is +38.8% to December 2027 and +65.4% to June 2029.

The shape of the return is the shape of the case: a narrow cone for earnings and a wide cone for the share price. The earnings are the floor; the multiple is the return. Every topic below keeps the two apart.

The earnings cone over the next eighteen months is narrow. FY27 EPS should land between about 148p and 163p at constant currency, around a base of 156.5p to 158p. Currency adds or subtracts about 3% of EPS for each 5% move in the dollar.

The share-price cone is wide, because the sector now sets RELX's price. RELX's peer basket explains half of RELX's daily price variance over the last six months (correlation 0.87 with Wolters Kluwer; beta 1.21 to the basket). Whether the multiple reaches 20.84x therefore depends about as much on bond yields and the sector's mood on AI as on RELX itself.

The market has three things wrong and one thing right.

1. The market prices the predictable part of the case as if it were the uncertain part.

Consensus EPS has not moved for six months, yet Buy ratings have fallen to 63% (down seven points in a month) and Morgan Stanley is at Equal-weight. Over the window, RELX's earnings rest on contracted price, controlled cost and a capital framework applied without exception since 2009.

2. The market debates the right question at the wrong time.

The right question is whether Legal's 10% growth is a peak. The test of that question is the second renewal of the AI-tier contracts in 2027 to 2029, which cannot be seen inside the window and will arrive in rounded figures when it does.

3. The second-order items the narrative ignores point up.

Print profit is falling at a third of the pace of print revenue; the FY28 margin gets an even-year Exhibitions step; and the brokers' currency assumptions (GBP/USD 1.33 to 1.37) sit above Morgan Stanley's forecast of 1.27, which would favour RELX's reported earnings.

What the market has right: there is no low bar to beat.

Estimates were never cut, so the share price needs either the multiple to recover or earnings to beat, and RELX beats only by small amounts.

Richard should not take the Phases page's 42% gap to the guideline multiple at face value. The Phases page measures the gap from 14.68x, which is September's reading at 2,496p carried forward. At 3,039p the same series reads about 18x, and the model's own price over forward EPS is 18.2x, so the true gap to 20.84x is 15% to 18%. The model's total shareholder return of +38.8% is still correct, because the model computes it from the end value rather than the starting multiple. The template's split of that return (multiple +41.7 points, earnings minus 5.1 points) is, however, an artefact of the stale starting multiple. The economic split is multiple about +14.5 points, earnings about +17 points and dividends +4.3 points (#11 and #12).

Five judgements move the shares most over one to two years. The table sizes each one against the FY27 base: revenue £10,673m, adjusted operating profit £3,854m (a 36.1% margin), net income £2,679m and EPS 158p. Two rules of thumb convert the arithmetic: each £10m of after-tax profit is about 0.4% of EPS, and each one-turn change in the multiple on FY29 EPS of 196p is about 6.4% of today's price.

The judgements on earnings net to small numbers; the judgement on the multiple does not. The plausible negatives on FY27 earnings sum to about minus 3% to minus 5%, and the plausible positives to about +3% to +4%, with currency adding plus or minus 3% on top. Judgement 1 (the multiple) moves the shares more than judgements 2 to 5 combined, and about half of judgement 1 lies outside RELX's control.

That asymmetry is what Richard is buying. The earnings floor grows 17% over eighteen months, so even a return to the trough multiple roughly gives back the capital. Against that floor sits a multiple whose normal level is 15% to 18% above today's.

Conclusion on the case. RELX is a high-quality compounder whose cause for concern (AI disintermediation) is clearing slowly while the shares sit on a bottom-quintile five-year multiple. The earnings are low-risk and the share price is not. The return over eighteen months is a call on the multiple, resting on an earnings floor that pays Richard to wait.

#1 The operating environment: external forces favour RELX's earnings and weigh on its multiple

The tailwinds act on revenue and profit now; the headwinds act on the multiple and on 2028 pricing.

Demand is improving structurally in the three divisions that make 88% of revenue, and is softening cyclically only in Exhibitions (12%). Legal growth accelerated from mid-single digits to 9% in FY25 and 10% in H1 26 and the first nine months of 2026. STM (scientific, technical and medical publishing) accelerated from 4% to 6%, and Risk is steady at 8%. Exhibitions slowed from 9% in H1 25 to 4% year to date, because Middle East tensions halved exhibitor numbers at the Arabian Travel Market.

Peers confirm the sector's strongest theme: professionals using AI still need trusted data, so database owners keep their customers and charge more at renewal. The October Sector Digest names that theme, and the peer evidence supports it. Thomson Reuters' Legal Professionals segment grew 10% in Q2 26 and 9% in Q3; Karnov's AI tiers carry 30% price uplifts; Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate Expert AI reached more than 90% of US enterprise health systems in nine months. Legal IT spend doubled from 2% to 4% of law-firm revenue between 2020 and 2025.

Input costs are turning into a tailwind. Token costs are below 1% of Legal's costs and AI model prices are deflating. AI coding assistants have kept RELX's organic headcount flat while product release frequency more than doubled. Two free inputs stay free: peer review remains unpaid (1.8 to 1.9 million reviewers), and public records remain open.

The headwinds are real and sit in two places: the Legal workflow interface and the discount rate.

First, well-funded entrants are contesting the Legal workflow interface. Harvey's annualised recurring revenue rose from $190m in December 2025 to more than $350m in late 2026, and Harvey raised $550m at a $15.5bn valuation in September. Legora doubled its annualised recurring revenue from $100m to $200m in under six months, raised $550m at $8.8bn in October, launched US primary legal research in August and introduced consumption pricing in June. Google launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal in August with Thomson Reuters, Harvey and Legora as partners and LexisNexis absent. Thomson Reuters plans consumption-pricing options from 2027.

Second, higher bond yields compress the multiple. The US ten-year yield is near 5.1%, with a December Fed hike more than 90% priced; gilt yields hit a post-2007 high of 5.44%. Morgan Stanley measured a correlation of minus 0.72 between software multiples and the US ten-year yield during the autumn sell-off.

The smaller headwinds are bounded. US grant rules on publication fees put at most about 70 basis points of STM revenue at risk, although sentiment trades the full 7% of group revenue with direct and indirect exposure. India's national subscription is a further small drag. Print revenue is running off at 15% to 17% a year, which takes about 0.6 points off reported revenue growth. Sterling's strength cut revenue by £291m in FY24 and £196m in FY25.

Inference: the AI threat has split in two, and only the weaker form has strengthened. The strong form of the threat (general AI models replace curated databases) has been disproved by the hallucination problem and by the entrants' own decision to license incumbent content. The weak form (AI-native front ends own the lawyer's workflow and move the pricing anchor away from seats) has strengthened. The weak form reaches RELX's numbers through renewal pricing on three-year contracts, so it is a 2028 to 2029 variable, not a 2027 one.

So what: the case does not need a particular macro outcome; it needs the AI fear to stop growing. External evidence supports the model's 7% underlying growth with rising margins for the window, while external forces drive the multiple. The macro contains a natural hedge: the same rate rises that compress the multiple also strengthen the dollar and lift RELX's reported EPS, and rate relief would do the reverse.

Strongest counter-case. The entrants are not only taking new workflow spend. A double-digit share of new small and mid-sized law-firm customers now goes to startups; DLA Piper rolled Harvey out to 5,000 lawyers and rates it ahead of Protégé; and law-firm chief information officers say rising spend on Harvey will eventually force cuts elsewhere. If that budget squeeze reaches the big-firm research line at the 2028 renewals, Legal's growth would return to the 2% to 5% of the years before 2024.

What would change my view. Thomson Reuters' Legal growth falling below 8% in any quarter (Thomson Reuters reports to one decimal place; RELX does not); an enterprise-wide displacement of Lexis by Harvey or Legora at a top-50 law firm; a US ten-year yield sustainably above 5.5%.

Market versus me. The market agrees with me on rates and is more bearish on AI than the eighteen-month evidence supports. The Assistant Portfolio Manager rates the sector C (weak), and RELX sits on the favourable side of every sector threat except the legal startups.

Conclusion. External forces favour RELX's earnings and disfavour its multiple. Structural demand and AI-driven pricing support 7% growth with rising margins through 2027, while the genuine headwinds (the legal interface and bond yields) bite on the multiple and on 2028 pricing, not on the window's profits.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. External forces are a clear, multi-part, structural net positive on the 88% of revenue outside Exhibitions: professionals using AI still need trusted data, so database owners keep customers and charge more at renewal (peers confirm it: Thomson Reuters Legal at 9-10%, Karnov AI tiers at +30%), law-firm IT spend doubled from 2% to 4% of revenue, STM demand rose from 4% to 6%, and falling model and token costs help margins. Against that sit a funded and direct threat at the Legal workflow layer (Harvey, Legora, Google), a cyclical Middle East dip in Exhibitions and small grant-rule and print drags; consensus sales growth at the 75th percentile is honest, but group organic growth is steady at about 7% rather than accelerating, so this is above Spie's favourable-but-mixed reading and below Helios Towers' broad structural pull, a touch above the 66 External change forces group because the forces reach nearly the whole perimeter.

#2 Internally driven change: broad, self-funded and already in the numbers; the risks are leadership and succession

RELX's core strategy is unchanged, but its ambition has widened from information to workflow. The strategy remains organic development of analytics and decision tools, small acquisitions, and buybacks as the balancing item. Erik Engstrom, the chief executive, now frames legal technology as a $75bn to $100bn market, against a $4bn to $5bn market for legal research alone.

Six internal forces for improvement are in motion.

ForceWhat has happened
AI sold as an upgrade to the proprietary database90% of Legal new-sales value and about 75% of US renewal value are on Lexis+ with Protégé; more than half of the US installed base has migrated; nearly 300 workflow tools exist, with two to three added each day
A larger buybackThe 2026 buyback was stepped up 50% to £2.25bn, of which £1.75bn was executed in H1 at an average of 2,529p, lifting leverage from 2.0x to 2.3x
Print exitPrint is reported as its own segment and is being exited through outsourcing and joint ventures
DoctrineAn acquisition of about £400m, closed on 14 August 2026, extending Legal into civil-law Europe and mid-tier firms
LeapSpaceA publisher-neutral research workspace in STM
Internal AI productivityOrganic headcount flat while release frequency more than doubled; an Agentic Content Platform in editorial

RELX funds all of this inside operating costs. Technology spend is about £2bn a year, and margins still rose 70 to 90 basis points a year while it was spent.

The internal negatives are present, but none is yet an earnings event.

  • Leadership concentration. Mark Kelsey retired as chief executive of Risk after 14 years, and Mike Walsh now runs both Legal and Risk, which together earn just over half of group profit. Deutsche Bank calls that concentration a clear operational risk.
  • No named successor. Erik Engstrom is 62 and has been chief executive since November 2009. The board says succession is a regular agenda item and gives no timetable; service contracts carry twelve months' notice.
  • Incentives that reward buybacks. The chief executive's maximum long-term incentive rose from 450% to 600% of salary and his annual incentive from 200% to 300%. Both reward EPS growth, which buybacks deliver mechanically.
  • Thinning disclosure. RELX reports divisional growth in whole numbers and divisional profit only half-yearly, with no price-volume split and no seat-linked or AI revenue. The nine-month statement also dropped the phrase "double-digit growth in law firms and corporate legal" that the Q1 and H1 statements carried.

Inference: RELX is strengthening an existing machine rather than building a new one. In the Wisdom Library's terms, RELX is a "Quality Compounder", not a "Massive Corporate Change Plan". The two largest changes (Legal AI monetisation and the step-up in capital returns) are already in the numbers. What is still to come is smaller: an agentic paid tier, LeapSpace monetisation, Doctrine's roll-out and continued productivity gains. Because the 2026 buyback used up the leverage headroom, 2027 capital returns will look lower even if capital allocation stays excellent.

So what: management quality justifies a high weight on the algorithm continuing, and the succession is a sentiment event for 2027 to 2029, not an earnings event. Peer precedents suggest first-year share-price volatility of two to three multiple turns around a chief-executive change, with earnings stable within 18 to 24 months. Wolters Kluwer fell 11% in one day on Nancy McKinstry's retirement announcement in February 2025, a day that coincided with AI fears; the Verisk and Pearson transitions were judged neutral. A new chief executive is also the likeliest route to better disclosure, which the market would reward.

Strongest counter-case. Engstrom's hands-on model (fortnightly reviews of individual profit-and-loss accounts) is what holds cost growth below revenue growth. A successor without that intimacy, combined with Walsh stretched across £5bn of revenue, could let the margin algorithm slip at exactly the moment Legal needs product velocity against Harvey.

What would change my view. A succession announcement naming an external candidate (which would reopen the risk to the capital framework); a decline in Legal's margin in FY26 (23.9% is expected; H1 was 21.7%, up 80 basis points); any sign that Protégé upgrades are being given away to hold renewals.

Market versus me. The market knows the buyback debate and Walsh's dual role. No broker note in the pack discusses succession, and none puts print's profit resilience (profit down 7% on revenue down 17% in H1 26) into its margin arithmetic. On balance, the narrative's omissions are slightly positive for the next eighteen months.

Conclusion. Internal change is broad, self-funded and already delivering (AI monetised at real prices, a record counter-cyclical buyback, the print exit), but the change is evolutionary. The live internal risks are leadership concentration and an unaddressed succession, and both are sentiment events rather than earnings events inside the window.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. RELX's own actions are broad, self-funded and already working: Lexis+ with Protégé carries 90% of Legal new-sales value at real prices with more than half the US base migrated, internal AI keeps headcount flat while release frequency doubled, the buyback was stepped up 50% at a low price, print is being exited and Doctrine and LeapSpace extend the reach, with the ambition widened from research to a $75-100bn workflow market. But it is an evolutionary strengthening of an existing machine whose largest moves are already in the numbers, offset by Walsh running both Legal and Risk, no named successor to a 62-year-old CEO of 17 years and disclosure that is getting thinner; that is more than Richard's 'gently positive but mediocre' CVS at 55 and in line with the 61 group, below OEM's active redeployment and just above Teqnion.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management: foundations as robust as any in Europe

RELX's industry structure is among the most supportive in listed markets, because RELX is number one or two in every business it runs.

  • STM: Elsevier publishes 22% of journal articles (Springer Nature 14%; the top five publishers hold 65%, a share that is rising).
  • Legal: US legal research is an 85% to 90% duopoly (Thomson Reuters about 55%, RELX 30% to 35%).
  • Risk: RELX holds near-monopolistic positions in insurance data and financial-crime compliance (49 of the top 50 banks are customers).
  • Exhibitions: RX is the global number two in exhibitions, behind Informa.

Every other force in the structure also favours RELX. Incumbents price on value and avoid price wars; prices held through 2009 and 2020. Suppliers are unpaid or powerless: reviewers, courts and registries, and in Risk the customers themselves, who must contribute data to more than 25 contributory databases in order to use them. Customers are diversified (the top 30 are under 30% of revenue). Regulators on balance raise barriers: explainability rules lock in Risk's models, the EU AI Act favours auditable data, and a court dismissed the antitrust suit over unpaid peer review in February 2026.

The one contested layer is legal workflow, where RELX is a fast follower with a hedge. Legal workflow is a market of about $25bn and is fragmented. RELX competes with its own interface and also distributes its content inside about 25 partner platforms, including Harvey, which receives about 1% of the database.

The moats are widening under AI, with one exception.

  • Content: curated, legally protected content and citation networks (more than 200 billion documents, four million added daily, and Shepard's citation service) are licensed by the very entrants the market fears will replace them.
  • Switching costs: high, through three-year contracts, retention above 95% in core analytics and months of security validation at banks.
  • Gatekeeping: STM's screening role gains value as AI-generated submissions rise (submissions are growing more than 20% against 7% growth in published articles).
  • Scale: technology spend of about £2bn a year, several times the entrants' combined revenue, funds AI inside normal budgets.

The exception is a position rather than a moat: ownership of the lawyer's screen. Harvey, Legora, Google and Microsoft are contesting that screen, and some large firms rate Protégé's user experience below Harvey's. A second soft spot is that RELX keeps most of its scale gains as margin rather than sharing them with customers, which invites undercutting at the bottom of the market.

RELX's financial profile is top-decile on every measure, and its one constraint is the mirror of that strength. The business cannot reinvest much more capital at high returns, so it returns 70% to 80% of free cash flow, and its fair multiple rests on durability rather than runway.

Management is a core strength, with two deductions: disclosure and succession (#2). Engstrom has cut print from 27% of revenue to 4%, delivered the algorithm for sixteen years, made only two large acquisitions and executed buybacks counter-cyclically; he holds shares worth about 26 times his salary. Nick Luff, finance director since 2014, is well regarded. The culture is finance-led and hands-on, summed up internally as "better, faster, cheaper". Management's goals are stretching in substance (compounding every year; the fastest platform migration in the company's history) but quiet in form: there are no numerical targets and no capital markets day, and communication is clear in message and thin in data.

Inference: the risk in the foundations is located precisely, and it is a pricing risk rather than a displacement risk. Structure, moat and financial profile together justify a base case of continued real price increases, high retention and mix-driven margin gains. The risk is not that content revenue is displaced; it is that Legal's pricing at renewal is constrained from 2028 if the industry moves from enterprise subscriptions to usage-based pricing.

So what: even the Legal bear case is "a paid supplier with slower growth", not a collapse. Legal is 19% of revenue and only about 12% to 13% of profit. Risk, at 36% of revenue and 39% of profit with 8% growth for years, is the engine the debate ignores.

Strongest counter-case. Thomson Reuters leads in research share, was a Gemini launch partner, sells Westlaw Advantage and CoCounsel as separate paid steps, and is moving first on consumption pricing. RELX instead bundles Protégé upgrades into the existing price, which helps penetration now but removes a monetisation step later. In a duopoly where RELX is the number two and most large firms buy from both suppliers, a budget squeeze lands on the number two first.

What would change my view. The loss of a top-50 firm's research contract to Thomson Reuters or a startup; Risk growth below 7% for two consecutive halves; a large acquisition (Taylor & Francis at about £3bn would take leverage to 2.4x and end the buyback for a year).

Market versus me. The market agrees on quality and over-weights Legal, which is 12% to 13% of profit yet the whole of the valuation debate. I would weight Risk's steadiness and STM's acceleration more heavily than the narrative does.

Conclusion. A fortress industry structure, widening content and data moats, a top-decile financial profile and an outstanding, aligned management make RELX's foundations as robust as any in European equities. The one contested position, the legal interface, is real but bounded at about an eighth of profit.

Score: 87, set by the Rater. None of the four parts is ordinary. The structure is number one or two everywhere, with an 85-90% US legal-research duopoly, near-monopoly contributory data in Risk and unpaid or powerless suppliers. The moats (curated content licensed even by the entrants, retention above 95%) are widening under AI, and returns on new capital are above 30%, which the figures confirm (ROIC 24.8% at the 94th percentile, margins at the 82nd to 84th, cash conversion 99%) and which are among the most predictable in Europe. Management has a sixteen-year record of delivery. I sit above the 78-80 groups because all four are strong at once and predictability adds to the quality, and I deduct for the contested legal interface (about an eighth of profit), the limited room to reinvest and the open succession; that puts it above Reply and Avanza, well short of ASML's monopoly bottleneck.

#4 Guidance: conservative in form, met in substance, never cut

RELX guides only in words, and has delivered under those words in every period of the last three years. The guidance sentence, unchanged since FY23 and repeated at the nine-month statement on 22 October 2026, promises "another year of strong underlying growth in revenue and adjusted operating profit, and strong growth in adjusted EPS at constant currency". Under that sentence RELX delivered underlying revenue growth of 8%, 7% and 7% and constant-currency EPS growth of about 10% (11% in H1 26).

RELX's misses against consensus came only from currency and disposals, never from operations. The two misses were FY23 revenue and FY24 EBIT. In H1 26 RELX beat consensus by 1.65% on adjusted EBIT and by 1.93% on EPS.

Upgrades arrive through wording and capital returns, never through numbers. In February 2026 RELX moved STM's outlook from "good to strong" to "strong", and set the buyback at £2.25bn against a consensus of about £1.3bn and Morgan Stanley's £1.75bn. Management's informal colour ("double acceleration"; legal technology as a $75bn to $100bn market) runs ahead of the formal sentence. The Change Forces report classifies Engstrom as a conservative sandbagger.

Inference: the guidance sentence will very likely be met and repeated, and only the buyback can surprise. FY26 guidance should be met at the upper end of what "strong" has meant (constant-currency EPS growth of 12% to 13% on the model). A verbal raise is unlikely because the words are already at the top of RELX's scale; a cut would need Legal growth below 7% or a shock to Risk's transactional revenue, and neither is close.

The February buyback is the one quantified item, so surprise in either direction sits there. My probabilities are £1.5bn about 25%, £1.75bn about 40% and £2.0bn or more about 35%. The case for the top outcome is that Fitch expects leverage at the upper end of RELX's range and that management's record is to use the range when the share price is low. Consensus share counts imply a buyback of about £2bn, so £1.75bn would be a small disappointment and £1.5bn a visible one.

So what: RELX's guidance style makes delivery predictable but makes guidance a weak early-warning signal. A deceleration would show first in a missing phrase rather than in the guidance sentence, as the nine-month statement's dropped "double-digit" Legal language already shows. Expectations are conservative in form (there are no numbers to beat) and fair in substance: consensus FY26 EPS is 141p against the model's 143p, and consensus FY27 EPS is 158p against the model's 158p. There is no kitchen-sinked bar. RELX's record is of small beats on the operating line and no beats below it, because tax and share count are set rather than managed.

Strongest counter-case. Thomson Reuters' Q3 26 margin guide came in more than 250 basis points below expectations because of token costs and CoCounsel marketing. Platform roll-outs can cost margin abruptly, and RELX's qualitative guidance style would let it absorb such a step without a formal cut while consensus margins fell.

What would change my view. A softer FY27 guidance sentence ("good" replacing "strong" for any division, or a Middle East caveat in the group outlook); a buyback of £1.5bn with deleveraging language; a Legal paragraph in February with no reference to double-digit law-firm growth.

Market versus me. Nobody expects a cut and nobody expects a verbal raise. I differ from the market on the buyback (I am below the consensus-implied £2bn and above Bernstein's £1.5bn) and on the FY26 margin (35.5% to 35.6% against consensus of 35.4%). The sell-side's tax rate (about 21% to 22% implied) and finance-cost assumptions are kinder than mine, which is why my FY27 EPS matches consensus despite my higher margin.

Conclusion. Guidance is conservative in form, consistently met in substance and never cut. The February buyback is the only number that can surprise, and the risk there is a small disappointment against an implied £2bn rather than a cut to the capital framework.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Over three years RELX met or beat in every period. The only misses against consensus came from currency and disposals, never from operations (H1 26 beat EBIT by 1.65% and EPS by 1.93%), and its de facto guidance ('strong growth' at constant currency) has never been cut outside 2020, with a sandbagging chief executive who turned the buyback into a raise well above consensus. It is held back because the upgrades come only in wording and capital returns, the beats are small, consensus sits level with what the company can deliver rather than below it, and the nine-month statement dropped its 'double-digit' Legal phrase. I am above the 56-60 groups because the absence of numbers is not itself negative; this sits just below Kerry's consistent banded delivery with raised targets and above Linea Directa.

#5 The business model's gearing: how 7% revenue growth becomes 10% to 12% EPS growth

Pricing power is demonstrated, and it is RELX's margin engine. Price contributes about 3.5 to 4 points of the 7% underlying growth in 2026; the table below shows the contribution and mechanism by division.

Price covers all of RELX's cost inflation and funds roughly the whole group margin gain. Costs of about £6.5bn inflate at 3% to 3.5%, which adds about £200m to £230m a year. Price on £9.7bn of continuing revenue adds £340m to £390m. The surplus of £120m to £170m is roughly the whole group margin gain, since each 10 basis points of margin is about £10m; volume growth then earns roughly the average margin.

The same arithmetic cuts both ways. A one-point fall in Legal's AI-tier uplift (about £20m of revenue) would cost about £20m of profit and 20 basis points of group margin, with almost no visible signal in group revenue. Price's contribution falls to about 3 to 3.5 points by 2028 as the one-time migration to the AI tier completes. That fade is why the model's margin expansion slows from 70 to 90 basis points a year to about 50 to 60.

Operating leverage is managed rather than mechanical. The incremental margin is about 45% (profit +9% on revenue +7%), because management sets cost growth (about 6%) below revenue growth in every division. The record shows the control works in downturns. In 2009 underlying revenue fell 6% and the group margin held at 25.9% through a 5.4% cost cut; in 2020 Exhibitions lost £164m and has since recovered to a 39% margin in H1 26. A one-point revenue miss with no cost response would cost about £48m of profit (1.4% of EPS), or about 1% with the usual partial cost response. Fifty basis points of margin is £53m (1.6% of EPS). Only Exhibitions has two-sided operating leverage.

Financial leverage adds less to EPS than it appears to. Buybacks retire about 3% of shares a year (3.1 points of gross EPS growth). But net debt rises £600m to £800m a year and refinances at 4.0% to 5.25% against a 3.6% average cost, so finance cost rises from £273m in FY25 to £375m in FY27 and £475m in FY30. That rise takes back 1.5 points of EPS growth in FY27 and about 1 point a year after.

The buyback's accretion shrinks as the share price rises. At £31 a share and FY27 EPS of about 156p, the earnings yield is 5.0%, against an after-tax marginal cost of debt of 3.6%. Each £1bn of buyback therefore adds only about 0.5% to EPS in its first full year, and a re-rating to 22x would cut that to near zero. The buyback is a balancing loop: the better the shares do, the less the buyback adds. Interest cover falls from 12x to about 10x, which is still comfortable, and 82% of borrowings are at fixed rates.

Cost-out is continuous rather than a programme. Staff costs are 32% of revenue. With headcount flat and wages up 2.5% to 3%, the gross productivity gain is worth 1.2 to 1.4 points of margin a year; about half is reinvested, and the rest, net of mix drags, reaches the group margin as 40 to 60 basis points a year. There is no restructuring to model and no easy programme left, because RELX already runs on shared technology. In a downturn, 5% to 10% of costs could come out within a year to protect margin, as in 2009.

The reverse risk is a forced step-up in AI investment. An extra point of revenue spent on AI (about £100m) would cost about 100 basis points of margin in the year of the step. Thomson Reuters' Q3 26 margin miss shows such a step can happen, and Wolters Kluwer is raising product development to 12% to 13% of revenue.

Feedback loops reinforce RELX's position now and start to balance it from 2028. Legal's acceleration is not a flywheel but a stock adjustment: each customer pays the AI-tier step once, at the renewal on which it migrates. The Karnov precedent (AI tier +30%, workflow tier a further +50%) shows that a price ladder is possible, but RELX has not yet priced the next rung. Mix drags of about 10 to 15 basis points a year explain why divisional margin gains of 50 to 90 basis points become a group gain of only about 50 to 60: Legal, the lowest-margin division at 23%, grows fastest, while print, at a 46% margin, runs off.

So what: delivery of the FY27 margin is the most likely source of a modest positive surprise, and a Legal price fade would show in margin before revenue. Revenue growth of 7% becomes operating profit growth of 8.5% to 9% and constant-currency EPS growth of 10% to 12%, year after year, with operating profit primary and the share count secondary. Because price above inflation is most of the margin gain, the model's FY27 margin of 36.1% (consensus 35.8%) is where RELX is most likely to beat.

Strongest counter-case. The AI-tier uplift is about 3 points of Legal growth and perhaps £40m a year of near-pure-margin revenue relative to 2026. As the uplift fades, about 35 basis points of group margin would disappear unless a new paid tier replaced it, and the model's margin gain of 50 basis points a year would become 15 to 25.

What would change my view. Legal's margin failing to rise in FY26 or H1 27; Legal growth falling from 10% while its margin stalls (a sign that the balancing loops are biting) rather than while its margin holds (a sign that the stock adjustment is simply ending); an explicit investment step in the February outlook.

Market versus me. The market counts the buyback at 3 to 4 points of EPS growth (the gross figure) and treats margin expansion as a given. I count the buyback at 1.5 to 2 points net of interest, and I treat margin as a price phenomenon with a fading component. Both differences are second-order for the window and the net EPS effect is the same, but RELX's sensitivity to Legal pricing is larger than the market's revenue-based framing implies.

Conclusion. RELX's model converts 7% revenue growth into 10% to 12% EPS growth through contracted price above cost inflation, managed operating leverage and buybacks at constant leverage. The gearing is reliable for eighteen months, and its weakest link, the one-time Legal price uplift, would show in margin first, from 2028.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Pricing power is proven and rare: price adds 3.5-4 points of the 7% growth, covers all of the 3-3.5% cost inflation and funds roughly the whole margin gain, and it held through 2009 and 2020. Reinforcing loops work in Risk's contributory data network and in STM gatekeeping. The other gears are ordinary: operating leverage is managed rather than mechanical (an incremental margin of about 45%, two-sided only in Exhibitions), cost-out is continuous with no programme left to run, and the buyback adds little net of a rising interest bill, so EPS grows about 1.5 times revenue, below the Universe's twice; strong on two elements with evidence puts it at the 75 level, trimmed because the one-time Legal tier uplift fades from 2028.

Behind the group, Legal's growth fades while Risk and STM hold, and every division's margin rises. Exhibitions' biennial cycle swings its reported growth between +2.5% and +9.0%. Print revenue falls 17% and then 15% a year, with profit falling at high single digits.

RELX can grow EPS at double digits in every forecast year. The algorithm gives EPS growth of 10% to 12.5% a year: reported operating profit growth of about 7.5% to 8.5%, minus 1 to 2 points for rising finance cost, plus 3 points from the falling share count, with the tax rate flat. FY27 is the weakest year (+10.7%), held back by the odd-year Exhibitions cycle, the Middle East, Doctrine's integration and a fading Legal uplift. FY28 is the strongest (+12.1%), with the even-year cycle and no comparable drag. At constant currency FY26 EPS grows 12% to 13%.

Growth and margins beat the past in reported terms but not in underlying terms. Reported EPS grew about 6.5% a year from FY19 to FY25 (78.9p to 115p on FactSet's diluted adjusted basis). That period absorbed Covid, a tax rate rising from 18.7% to 24.8% (about 7% of EPS) and currency drags of 2 to 3 points a year. The forecast's 10.5% to 11% a year is the same business without those headwinds, with a buyback about 50% larger, less a rising interest bill. About two-thirds of the gap between the model's FY30 EPS and a simple extrapolation of the FY23 to FY25 reported growth rate comes from the assumption that sterling stops subtracting.

The margin reaches a record level but rises more slowly than before. Underlying revenue growth drifts from 7% to 6.4% as Legal's migration ends. The margin climbs from 34.8% to 37.8% by FY30, but at 50 to 60 basis points a year against 80 to 90 in the past. The honest description is "the same compounding, reported more cleanly", not "an acceleration".

The model differs from consensus in shape, not in level. The model is in line with consensus on revenue to FY28 (within 1%). It is above consensus on EBIT (+0.4%, +0.4% and +1.6%), because consensus margins flatten at 35.8% in FY28 against the model's 36.7%. It is below consensus on net income, because the model's tax rate is 23% against an implied 21% to 22%, and its FY27 finance cost is higher than the brokers' £324m to £354m (though lower than the consensus-implied £405m). The two effects cancel, so EPS is equal.

FY29 consensus should rise 2% to 3% as coverage fills in, as a coverage artefact rather than momentum. FY29 consensus rests on one broker (189p), and the model's 196p and the Analyst's 193p both sit above it.

#7 Scope for upgrades over 6 to 12 months: modest for earnings; the upgrade that matters is to the multiple

The sell-side agrees about RELX's business and disagrees only about translation, buyback and tax. Consensus FY27 EPS (a median of 158p across 13 brokers, range 151p to 163p) has not moved for six months and is up 2.2% over twelve. Over twelve months, consensus FY27 sales are down 3% and EBITDA down 1%, both because of currency. The 8% spread across brokers comes almost entirely from currency assumptions (GBP/USD 1.33 to 1.37), the buyback (from £1.5bn at £25 a share for Bernstein to £2.07bn for Rothschild & Co Redburn) and tax, not from views on operations.

Target prices are edging up, and the weak sell-side readings reflect rating drift rather than estimate pressure. Mean target prices are up 1% over one month and 3% over three (mean 3,394p, median 3,262p). Bernstein raised its target to 3,760p on 28 October; Deutsche Bank is at 3,100p, Redburn at 3,500p and Morgan Stanley at 2,990p. The dashboard's sell-side momentum letter is D and its revision score minus 3, because ratings drifted down as the price approached targets.

Strongest counter-case. The market expects estimates to stay flat; I expect them to stay flat with a mild upward drift.

Conclusion. Earnings upgrades over six to twelve months are modest (zero to +3%) and will be decided by the dollar and the February buyback. The upgrade that matters is to the multiple, and it needs time without a miss rather than a single print that proves the thesis.

#8 Current momentum: a pre-momentum entry, with the sector setting the timing

Guidance momentum is neutral. RELX held its guidance at nine months. The only recent change in wording is the dropped "double-digit" Legal phrase, which is mildly negative, and the last upgrade was the buyback in February 2026.

Estimate momentum is flat. FY27 EPS revisions are 0% over one, three and six months and +2% over twelve: no cuts and no raises for half a year. The broker count is full (13) and the estimates are tightly grouped.

Narrative momentum is improving slowly from a bearish tilt. The story has moved from "AI destroys RELX" in February to "AI is a growth catalyst, but is it temporary?", the question in Morgan Stanley's September note "Why hasn't RELX rallied more strongly?". Investor behaviour is split. BlackRock's Unconstrained Equity Fund and its Greater Europe trust sold; the trust's sale, reported on 3 November 2026, cited "little appetite for earnings disappointments given the genuine unknowns". Brunner and BlackRock Income & Growth added on weakness, and Quilter wrote "RELX brushes off the SaaSpocalypse" after H1.

Bernstein's 28 October note is a bull argument presented as a measurement. After adjusting for rates, Bernstein finds that only RELX, Wolters Kluwer and Thomson Reuters still carry a residual AI risk premium of up to two points of free-cash-flow yield. Meanwhile the Buy share of ratings is 63%, down seven points in a month, and Morgan Stanley has been at Equal-weight since May.

Price momentum is recovering but not yet confirmed. The price is 18.9% above its 200-day average of 2,555p, but that average has risen in none of the last twelve months. The relative-strength percentile is 57 and the 52-week range is 1,990p to 3,538p. The dashboard letters are C for technicals, D for sell-side and A for valuation. Short interest is only 0.3% of shares, so there is no short-covering fuel.

Inference: RELX should be first in line when the sector turns. RELX was also the first name to trigger the Stage 1 Speculative Bet test, at the February low.

So what: this is a pre-momentum entry, not a momentum entry. The weak technical and sell-side readings are the signatures of a stock whose estimates have held while its multiple has not yet recovered half its fall. The peer evidence says the sector factor, not the company, will decide the next three months.

Strongest counter-case. A rebound in the AI complex could rotate money out of the UK's low-AI, low-beta trade, since the UK index's recent outperformance is a factor outcome. Fitness for Fighting has the Momentum tilt at Underweight and sees risk-off broadening. And a disappointment at Wolters Kluwer or Experian would move RELX on the day, whatever RELX reports.

What would change my view. The 200-day average turning up with the price holding above 2,900p (confirmation); a break below the 50-day average (2,628p) on a peer event (the sector factor reasserting itself).

Market versus me. I agree with the readings and disagree with their implication. A D in sell-side momentum here means ratings drifting down as the price rose towards targets, which is what a re-rating looks like from inside the ratings data.

Conclusion. Momentum is flat in estimates, weak in ratings, recovering but unconfirmed in price and improving in narrative. RELX is trading as a 1.2-beta member of a de-rated peer group rather than on its own delivery.

FY27 revisions have been 0% for six months, the share of Buy ratings fell seven points in a month, the guidance wording lost its double-digit Legal phrase, and the 200-day average has not risen in twelve months despite the price sitting 19% above it after a 13% three-month rise. The narrative is improving slowly, and the comparable peer group (Wolters Kluwer, Experian, Informa) is de-rated and weak.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity: simple, low-risk fundamentals inside a high-risk share price

The market treats RELX as risky because of AI; the evidence says the fundamentals are simple and low-risk for eighteen months, and the share price is high-risk because half its variance now belongs to the sector. Both statements are true at once, and the market has them inverted.

The case is simple: three numbers describe the fundamentals and three variables carry almost all the forecast variance. The three numbers are 7% underlying revenue growth, 9% underlying operating profit growth and 10% to 12% constant-currency EPS growth. The three variables are sterling, margin delivery and Legal's price at the second renewal.

RELX's operating drivers are diffuse, which keeps the earnings cone narrow. RELX has four divisions, no customer above a few per cent of revenue, and price increases spread across escalators, transformative agreements, AI tiers and exhibition stands. That diffusion is why the constant-currency FY27 EPS cone is only minus 5% to +4%. RELX has already demonstrated everything the forecast needs for eighteen months. The one strength RELX has not demonstrated is holding a priced AI tier through a second renewal, against funded entrants and a competitor moving to consumption pricing, and that is an FY28 to FY30 variable.

The forecast requires six things, none of them new. It requires no translation drag; a February buyback at or above £1.5bn; cost growth kept below revenue growth; Legal growth of 9% in FY27; Exhibitions rebooking at 4%; and no strengthening of sterling against the dollar.

The forecast does not require a second paid tier, consumption-pricing capability, a leading workflow interface or elite AI talent at scale. Those are bull-case items, and their absence is the bear case's mechanism. The one disclosed but unmodelled structural item is a print sale: Thomson Reuters sold 51% of its print business to KKR at 5.3x EBITDA on 1 October 2026, and a RELX print sale would cost about 2% to 3% of EPS, with low probability inside eighteen months.

Share-price risk is sudden, hard to track and material. RELX's price fell 14.7% in a day on a competitor's launch. Peer results move RELX on the day: Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate renewals and its margin after a 12% to 13% product-development step, Experian's consumer credit and Thomson Reuters' quarters. Bond yields move the multiple on the same day, and a succession announcement would be a sudden sentiment event.

RELX's thin disclosure makes its own risks untrackable between results, so monitoring must be external. A Legal slowdown from 10.4% to 9.5% would stay invisible until a half-year figure rounded down, and change shows in wording before numbers. I would monitor, in this order:

  1. the Legal wording and growth figure in February;
  2. the size of the 2027 buyback;
  3. the FY26 margin against 35.5%;
  4. Thomson Reuters' Q4 Legal growth and pricing commentary;
  5. the dollar;
  6. Exhibitions' rebooking, and the Arabian Travel Market exhibitor count in May;
  7. the LexisNexis Insurance Demand Meter, for Risk's auto-insurance volumes;
  8. Harvey and Legora milestones.

Cyclicality is limited. 54% of revenue is subscription and most of the rest is machine-to-machine transactional revenue; litigation and bankruptcy work is counter-cyclical; and Exhibitions (12%) is the only cyclical division. Morgan Stanley's bear case takes Risk to mid-single-digit growth in a severe US slowdown, which on that reading makes about 20% of group revenue macro-sensitive. In 2009 underlying revenue fell 6% and the margin held. In 2020 revenue fell 9.7% because trade shows closed, the buyback was suspended at £150m, and the multiple troughed at 15.4x before reaching 21.6x by December 2021.

Every prior sector de-rating recovered to 18x to 24x within twelve to eighteen months. Each recovery came on earnings delivery, a capital return and a pause in yields, and each prior bear argument about the content (internet disintermediation, open access) proved wrong. European software de-rated 25% in 2022 against 62% in the US, so quality European compounders had relative support. Rothschild & Co Redburn's rule of thumb is that stocks that keep strong estimate momentum see their multiples recover within nine to twelve months.

The share-price cone to December 2027 is wide (minus 35% to +47%), but it has more room above than below today's multiple. The matrix below values the shares on FY29 EPS plus 131p of dividends. Two further cases sit outside it: bear-case earnings (FY29 EPS about 7% lower) at a 15x multiple give about 2,860p (minus 6%), and Morgan Stanley's severe bear (13x on cut earnings) gives about 1,900p to 2,100p (minus 30% to minus 38%).

The only route to a large loss is an earnings cut and a trough multiple together, and RELX's contracts make an earnings cut unlikely in 2027.

The case is not a macro bet in either direction, because rates and the dollar offset each other. A Fed that keeps hiking compresses RELX's multiple but lifts its reported EPS through a stronger dollar; rate relief re-rates the sector but weakens the dollar. The case's macro exposure is instead to bond volatility, which Morgan Stanley finds a bigger driver of repricing than the level of yields, and to the AI factor.

Strongest counter-case. The earnings cone and the share-price cone can merge. If the market reads a peer event as evidence on RELX's pricing model (Wolters Kluwer losing UpToDate business to OpenEvidence, or a Thomson Reuters consumption-pricing offer that law firms embrace), the multiple can fall to 14x while estimates are untouched, and RELX's half-yearly reporting cadence gives it no means to answer for months.

What would change my view. Any Legal half-year growth figure below 8%; cash conversion below 95%; a slowdown in Risk's transactional revenue visible in the Demand Meter; an enterprise contract at a top-50 firm moving from fixed to consumption pricing.

Market versus me. The market prices RELX's fundamentals as the risky part and its share price as the safe part. I think the reverse holds for the next eighteen months: the fundamentals are simple and low-risk, and the share price is high-risk because the sector now explains half its variance.

Conclusion. The case is simple and low-risk in its fundamentals (three drivers, a narrow earnings cone, sixteen years of precedent) and high-risk in its share price (sudden, externally triggered and poorly trackable moves, on a 1.2 beta to a de-rated group). The decisive fundamental test lies outside the window.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. The fundamentals are simple and low-risk. Three drivers (sterling, margin delivery and Legal price at the second renewal, which falls outside the window), a constant-currency FY27 EPS cone of about -5% to +4% (plus or minus 3% for the dollar), low cyclicality with only Exhibitions' 12% cyclical, and leverage of about 2x with 82% of debt fixed, which is moderate rather than minimal. The share-price risk is high, sudden and poorly trackable: a 14.7% one-day fall on a competitor's launch, a beta of 1.2 to a de-rated peer group that explains half the variance, and half-yearly, rounded disclosure that hides a Legal slowdown until it lands. I score above the 58 first-layer Risks group and near the 70 third-and-fourth-layer group, below Imperial Brands' slow, predictable decline and above OEM International.

#10 Lifecycle: turning up, with the thesis beginning to broaden

The Phases page's rule puts RELX in "Broadening", with a guideline multiple at the 80th percentile of its ten-year history. The data support that call in six ways:

  • estimates have held for six months after a reset in multiples rather than earnings, so there was never an earnings cut to recover from;
  • the price is 51% above the low, and the multiple has recovered from 14.3x to about 18x, roughly the ten-year median and still the bottom quintile of five years;
  • Buy ratings are falling as the price nears targets;
  • the narrative has moved from existential threat to "temporary acceleration?";
  • the 200-day average has not yet turned up;
  • the catalysts ahead are confirmations (February and July 2027) rather than proofs (late 2027 to 2029).

Inference: I place RELX between "turning up" and the early edge of "thesis broadening" on the six-phase scale. The earnings are in a reinforcing phase, with the algorithm delivering at the top of its range. The price has turned up but is not confirmed. The thesis has not yet broadened, because the market still debates the one question that cannot be answered inside the window. The dashboard's "Broadening" is defensible on the price and estimate data; I would call it early Broadening, with the proviso that the multiple is 15% to 18% below the guideline rather than the 42% the stale Phases figure shows.

So what for the fair multiple: anchor at 18.5x to 20.4x for the next year and treat 20.84x as the destination. A stock that is turning up with uncertain forecasts normally earns a lower multiple than one in peak delivery. RELX's forecasts are not uncertain for eighteen months, so the discount that the phase implies should be small. That argues for an anchor between the ten-year median and the 75th percentile (18.5x to 20.4x) over the next year, and for the 80th percentile (20.84x) once the second-renewal evidence lands.

Strongest counter-case. "Stalling" fits several of the readings: ratings are drifting down (Buy share down seven points), RELX has performed only in line with its peer basket despite a beat, and Legal's growth is at the top of its range with its acceleration about to slow. If Legal prints 9% in February and the buyback is £1.5bn, the market would read the stock as stalling even with the algorithm intact.

What would change my view. Up: an H1 27 margin beat with Legal at 9% or better and a rising 200-day average (Broadening confirmed). Down: Legal at 8% in April with no "double-digit" reference, or a Thomson Reuters Legal quarter below 8% (Stalling).

Market versus me. I am closer to the dashboard's Broadening than to either investor camp (the sceptics' "peak" and the holders' "quality at a discount, waiting"). What the sceptics call a peak is a one-time stock adjustment that the model already fades.

Conclusion. RELX is turning up, with its earnings reinforcing and its thesis beginning, but not yet confirmed, to broaden. The phase justifies a multiple near the ten-year median now and the 80th percentile as the destination.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. The memo's 'between turning up and early Broadening' is generous on the thesis and right on the price. The share price and multiple have turned up from a sentiment trough (+51% from the low, from 14.3x to about 18x), but the fundamentals are in steady mid-cycle Reinforcing: underlying growth flat at 7%, estimates unmoved for six months at the 45th percentile, Buy ratings falling, and the 200-day average not yet rising. Nothing is accelerating into growth, guidance or forecasts, and the catalysts ahead are confirmations rather than proofs. So the computed Broadening runs ahead of the evidence; this sits just below Kerry's mid-cycle Reinforcing and just above Banca Generali's late Reinforcing, with the turn in the multiple as what lifts it.

#11 The fair multiple: 20.84x is the right destination and a demanding eighteen-month target

Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the Broadening phase is 20.84x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of RELX's own ten-year monthly history. That history runs from 14.3x (June 2026) to 27.1x (April 2025), with a 10th percentile of 15.4x, a median of 18.5x, a 75th percentile of 20.4x and a 90th percentile of 22.2x. The five-year median is 20.9x, so the guideline is also the normal multiple of the last five years.

Today's multiple on the same basis is about 18x. The model gives 18.2x on the average of FY27 and FY28 EPS. FactSet's rolling 24-month-forward multiple is 17.66x, the 15th percentile of five years and the 36th of two.

The brokers' and peers' reference points bracket the guideline. Bernstein's intrinsic-value matrix gives 22.4x at a 5% riskless rate and a beta of 0.8. Morgan Stanley's bull case of 3,660p is about 23x FY27 EPS, and its bear case is 13x to 14x. Bernstein's target of 3,760p is about 23.5x its FY27 EPS of 160p, and the mean target of 3,394p is about 20x the average of FY27 and FY28 EPS. On Bernstein's 2027 numbers, Thomson Reuters trades at 25x, Verisk at 23x, Experian at 19x and Wolters Kluwer at 14x.

20.84x is the right destination, for three reasons. First, it is the level the stock has regained every time a de-rating cleared (18x to 24x after every prior episode). Second, at 20.84x the FY27 free-cash-flow yield would still be about 4.4%, on a business growing 7% with 100% cash conversion. Third, Bernstein's rate-adjusted work finds that RELX still carries a residual AI premium of up to two points of yield with no counterpart in its earnings.

20.84x is also a demanding eighteen-month target, for two reasons. First, reaching 20.84x inside eighteen months needs either a sector re-rating (rate relief or a fading AI fear, both outside RELX's control) or company evidence that cannot arrive before July 2027 and will be rounded when it does. Second, 20.84x is at the top of the ten-year range if the 2021 to 2025 period is excluded, and in that period the sector was priced for a lower discount rate.

My anchor for the next twelve months is 19x to 20x, between the ten-year median and the 75th percentile, which is what the market already pays in its targets. I expect the stock to trade at 20.84x once the first AI-tier renewal cohort passes without a visible give-back, in late 2027 to 2028.

The multiple does not need a Legal acceleration; it needs the absence of a Legal break. The structural de-rating scenario (Morgan Stanley's 13x on 4.5% growth and low-30s margins) is the one scenario that would make 20.84x permanently wrong, and it needs the second renewal to fail, which is a 2028 event. In the 2016, 2020 and 2022 episodes, capital returns at low multiples (the £700m buyback of 2017 and the £1bn of 2024) and a pause in yields marked the turn. A large capital return is present now, and a pause in yields is plausible.

Strongest counter-case. Bernstein notes that free-cash-flow yield is a better lens than P/E through de-ratings because it captures the debt. At 2.2x leverage and with a rising interest bill, the yield on RELX's equity is more sensitive to rates than the multiple history suggests. Morgan Stanley's regression has a US ten-year yield of 5% implying 12% downside to the multiple, against a yield of 4% to 4.99% implying only 3% upside. That rates asymmetry argues for a lower anchor than 20.84x while the ten-year yield is above 5%.

What would change my view. A US ten-year yield back below 4.5% with RELX's estimates intact (20.84x would become a twelve-month target); a Legal half-year at or below 8% (the anchor would fall to the ten-year median of 18.5x until the cause is clear).

Market versus me. The market's targets imply about 20x, and the Phases page shows 42% upside to the guideline; the true upside is 15% to 18%. I think the market has the multiple about right for now and will pay the guideline when the proof arrives.

Conclusion. The guideline fair multiple of 20.84x is the right normal level for a stock whose cause for concern has cleared, and it is 15% to 18% above today's multiple of about 18x, not 42%. I anchor at 19x to 20x for the coming year and at the guideline from late 2027, when the first second-renewal evidence can land.

#12 Total shareholder return at the guideline multiple: +39% in eighteen months, of which about 60% is earnings and dividends

At 20.84x the model gives a total shareholder return of +38.8% to 31 December 2027 and +65.4% to 30 June 2029. The eighteen-month figure is 32.0% annualised, on a value per share of £42.20; the three-year figure is 20.6% annualised, on £50.25.

The template's split of that return credits the multiple with the whole of it, and that split is wrong. The template's Dupont split for eighteen months is dividends +4.3 points, multiple +41.7 and earnings minus 5.1; for three years it is dividends +7.1, multiple +41.3 and earnings +12.0.

The model's totals are robust, because each is built from an end value. The end value is the guideline multiple applied to EPS two years forward from the column date, plus accumulated dividends. At December 2027 that is 20.84 x 196p (FY29) = 4,085p, plus about 131p of dividends = 4,216p, or +39% on today's 3,039p. At June 2029 it is 20.84 x about 231p (the FY30 to FY31 blend) = 4,810p, plus about 216p of dividends = 5,025p, or +65%.

The template's attribution misleads because it starts from the stale multiple. The template measures the multiple's change from the Phases page's 14.68x (September's reading at 2,496p) to 20.84x, which is +42%, and books the residual as "earnings". That residual comes out negative because the real starting multiple is 18.2x.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

RELX is a fortress-structure compounder whose earnings over the next eighteen months are as predictable as any in Europe, and whose share price has been handed to a sector factor it does not control.

The business will deliver about 7% underlying growth, a margin above 36%, double-digit EPS growth, 100% cash conversion and about 5.7% of its market value back to shareholders in 2027. It will report that delivery twice a year in rounded, half-yearly prose that gives the sceptics nothing to seize and the believers nothing to brandish.

The cause for concern, that AI-native tools will reprice Legal's commercial model at renewal, is legitimate, bounded (an eighth of profit) and lagged (2028 to 2029). On all precedent it is the kind of argument RELX has beaten before. It is, however, the first bear case aimed at RELX's pricing model rather than its content, so the record cannot settle it, and the market will accept the answer on evidence rather than on faith.

The investment case is therefore a multiple-reversion case on a growing floor. At about 18x the stock is at its ten-year median and the bottom of its five-year range, and the guideline of 20.84x is 15% to 18% higher. Earnings and dividends add about 20% over eighteen months whatever the multiple does, and the plausible downside needs a trough multiple and an earnings cut together, which RELX's contracts make unlikely inside the window.

The near-term path runs through 18 February 2027 (the buyback, the margin and the Legal wording), July 2027 (the H1 margin step) and the sector's mood on rates and AI, which decides about half of the outcome.

What Richard is paid for is patience with a company that does not miss, during a period in which the market has mistaken a slow proof for a live risk.

The input forces are clearly positive and very likely to reach profits: external pricing and demand at 72, internal AI monetisation, productivity and capital return at 62, and contracted price and controlled cost behind them. But the financial output is only moderately better than typical: about 11% EPS growth (B, consensus at the 56th percentile) is the past's compounding reported more cleanly rather than a step-up, with margin expansion slowing. That makes it a firm but mild net positive in the 60s, short of the 75 level, which needs profit growth well above the typical company's.

Foundations' Robustness: 90, set by the Rater. Quality of the business at 87 is a top-decile franchise on every part (oligopoly structure, moats widening under AI, top-decile returns and 99% cash conversion, outstanding management). The delivery record at 72 matches it in substance: sixteen years of the algorithm and no operational cut in three years, though without formal raises. That clearly beats Richard's CVS Group at 80 on structure, returns and predictability; it is held off the very top only by 2x leverage rather than net cash, the contested legal interface and the open succession.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 76, set by the Rater. The case fits 'CfC Clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a Q1/Q2 multiple, leading to reversion to normal' (CfC: cause for concern) clearly on quality and low cyclicality, where it is a better business than Richard's CVS Group at 65-75 for the same setup. Two elements are loose in substance: the cause for concern is clearing only in its strong form (general models replacing databases) while its weak form (AI front ends moving pricing away from seats) has strengthened and is settled only at the 2027-2029 renewals, and the multiple is in the bottom quintile of five years but only at the median of ten. That puts it at the 75 level of a quality business with its cause for concern clearing, with no current operating problem to pull it lower.

Case Riskiness: 73, set by the Rater. The fundamental risks are Richard's 'paper cuts': a narrow constant-currency cone, three drivers, low cyclicality and a conservatively guiding management, with a multiple low in its five-year range, which on its own argues for the 80s (CVS Group 80-85). But the share price is carried by a sector theme (the AI factor and bond yields, a 1.2 beta, a 14.7% one-day fall), and thin half-yearly disclosure delays the company's answer. That pulls it towards Arteche's 60 without the very high multiple, so it sits just above Riskiness and simplicity at 68.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
